profile.name: Furong Jia
profile.description: Furong Jia is a Computer Science Ph.D. student at Duke University studying how data shapes LLM behavior and how LLMs interpret data, with interests in probabilistic knowledge, AI agents, and AI for healthcare.

about: Hi! I am a third-year Computer Science PhD student at Duke University, supervised by Prof. Monica Agrawal. Previously, I received a B.S. in Computer Science and a B.S. in Applied and Computational Mathematics from University of Southern California, where I was fortunate to work with Prof. Yan Liu, Prof. Jesse Thomason, and Prof. Maja Matarić.

Research: I study how data shapes LLM behavior and how LLMs interpret data, with the broader goal of understanding what makes these systems reliable, interpretable, and robust. My work examines how pretraining data and inference-time inputs influence model reasoning, including how faithfully LLMs acquire probabilistic knowledge from text. My research also spans diverse data (text, time series, and multimodal inputs), including developing forecasting methods and studying model behavior under distribution shift. More recently, I have been investigating how LLMs identify and explain distributional differences between text corpora, and whether different agent harnesses affect performance in scientific discovery. I am also interested in human–agent interaction, particularly when and how agents should seek human input. My broader application interests lie in AI for healthcare, where generalizability and responsible deployment are especially important.
Feel free to reach out to me if you'd like to discuss research or explore potential collaboration!

projects.title: When does the harness matter for LLM-driven discovery?
bullets: Led a controlled comparison of 11 LLM search harnesses, from best-of-N sampling to evolutionary search and coding agents, on math construction, GPU kernel optimization, and nanoGPT training, under a shared task interface, evaluators, and API-cost ledger.
Found that choosing a harness often mattered more than upgrading the model, but the best harness depends on the setup: rankings change with how the budget is measured and which model is used.

projects.title: How faithfully do LLMs acquire probabilistic knowledge?
bullets: Continually pretrained OLMo-2 1B and 7B on millions of notes generated from 650 synthetic Bayesian networks, so learned probabilities can be checked exactly.

Found relational compression: models get individual probabilities about right and rank outcomes correctly, yet understate how far apart outcomes are and how much strong evidence should shift a prediction. Standard metrics miss this.

projects.title: How do LLMs learn clinical knowledge?
bullets: Built MedLingo, a jargon benchmark from real clinical notes, and showed that term–meaning co-occurrence counts in pretraining corpora predict which jargon a model understands; jargon common in clinical notes is often rare in pretraining data.
Models reject disputed medical claims when asked directly but are far likelier to endorse them when the question presupposes them.

projects.title: Can counting match an LLM?
bullets: Introduced FBPR, a Naive Bayes that ranks MedQA diagnoses using concept–diagnosis co-occurrence counts from an LLM's pretraining corpus; it matches that LLM's diagnostic accuracy (OLMo 7B, LLaMA 65B).
The two get largely different questions right, so LLMs are not simply aggregating frequencies, and a simple hybrid of the two beats both.

projects.title: Interpreting dataset shift in clinical notes
bullets: Built a benchmark that induces controlled shifts in real MIMIC-IV notes, and SIReNs, which explains a shift by showing an LLM representative notes from each dataset.
SIReNs nearly matches an oracle on clear-cut binary shifts but struggles with gradual continuous ones. Now extending this to LLM agents and harnesses on multifactorial shifts.

projects.title: GPT4MTS: Prompt-Based Large Language Model for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting
bullets: Built an LLM pipeline that pairs time series with related news summaries and used it to create a GDELT news-coverage dataset for 55 U.S. regions.
Feeding the text to GPT-2 as soft prompts cut MSE by 4% over the best LLM baseline.

projects.title: TEMPO: Prompt-based Generative Pre-trained Transformer for Time Series Forecasting
bullets: Co-developed and ran training experiments for a GPT-2 forecaster that splits each series into trend, seasonal, and residual parts and uses prompts to adapt to distribution shift.
In zero-shot forecasting on unseen datasets, it outperformed baselines evaluated the same way (e.g., 19% lower MAE than PatchTST on ETTm1).

projects.title: I2I: Initializing Adapters with Improvised Knowledge
bullets: Trained CLIP-BART for a method that starts each new task's adapter from a distilled blend of earlier ones.
On five VQA tasks it raised new-task scores 4% relative to independent adapters, while AdapterFusion lowered them 2%: reuse works best as a starting point.
